Title (verbatim): AUTHOR'S PURPOSE
Copy (verbatim):
Why did the author write this?
PERSUADE — Convince you to agree or act.
Clues: opinions, reasons, evidence.
INFORM — Teach facts about a topic.
Clues: facts, explanations, examples.
ENTERTAIN — Engage you with a story.
Clues: characters, events, humor.
EXPLAIN — Show how or why.
Often a type of informing.
READ → FIND CLUES → NAME THE MAIN PURPOSE
A text may have more than one purpose.
Illustration and layout: Four illustrated panels: child campaigning for school garden; inventor explaining telephone; amusing rabbit and lizard storybook; hands following planting steps.

Title (verbatim): TEXT STRUCTURE
Copy (verbatim):
How are the ideas organized?
DESCRIPTION — Topic + details
SEQUENCE — First → Next → Finally
CAUSE & EFFECT — Why → Result
COMPARE & CONTRAST — Alike + Different
PROBLEM & SOLUTION — Difficulty → Response
Look at how ideas connect, not just clue words.
Illustration and layout: Five clear stacked panels each with diagram and tiny scene: flower and details; seed growth sequence; rain causes puddle; two bicycles same/different; broken bridge and repaired bridge.

Title (verbatim): FIGURATIVE LANGUAGE
Copy (verbatim):
Words that help us imagine and feel
SIMILE — Compares using like or as.
Her smile was like sunshine.
METAPHOR — Describes one thing as another.
The classroom was a zoo.
PERSONIFICATION — Gives human qualities to nonhuman things.
The wind whispered.
HYPERBOLE — Exaggerates for effect.
I waited a million years.
IDIOM — A phrase with a special meaning.
A piece of cake = easy.
Name it → Explain its meaning → Describe its effect
Illustration and layout: Five memorable illustrated panels connected to each expression. Clear text is main focus.

Title (verbatim): CENTRAL IDEA
Copy (verbatim):
The most important point about a topic
TOPIC — What is it about?
Bees
CENTRAL IDEA — What does the author say?
Bees help plants reproduce by moving pollen.
SUPPORTING DETAILS
Bees carry pollen between flowers.
Pollination helps many plants make seeds.
Many crops depend on pollinators.
Find a full sentence that connects the key details.
One detail is too narrow.
Illustration and layout: A bee garden illustration and clear tree diagram: topic at top central idea trunk three supporting-detail branches. Arrows hierarchy unambiguous.

Title (verbatim): POINT OF VIEW
Copy (verbatim):
Who tells the story? Whose thoughts do we know?
FIRST PERSON — A character tells the story.
I, me, we, our
THIRD-PERSON LIMITED — An outside narrator reveals one mind.
THIRD-PERSON OMNISCIENT — An outside narrator can reveal many minds.
THIRD-PERSON OBJECTIVE — An outside narrator reports actions and dialogue, not inner thoughts.
Read the narration outside quotation marks.
An I in dialogue does not make the story first person.
Illustration and layout: Four clearly separated panels visualizing narrator child own thought; outside narrator spotlight one thought; outside narrator multiple thought bubbles; camera records actions and speech without thought bubbles.

Title (verbatim): IDEAS AND SUPPORT
Copy (verbatim):
Build a strong argument
CLAIM — What should we believe?
Schools should support young inventors.
REASON — Why does it make sense?
Invention projects teach problem-solving.
EVIDENCE — What specific detail supports it?
Students test models and improve designs that fail.
EXPLANATION — How does the evidence connect?
Testing and improving designs practices problem-solving.
CLAIM → REASON → EVIDENCE → EXPLANATION
Choose support that fits the claim.
Illustration and layout: Building-block or bridge diagram with four steps, young inventor testing a cardboard vehicle. Exact copy in spacious stacked panels.

Title (verbatim): TEXT EVIDENCE
Copy (verbatim):
Prove your answer with the passage
ANSWER — State your idea.
Noor is helpful.
EVIDENCE — Choose a relevant detail.
She stops playing to carry her neighbor's bags.
EXPLAIN — Connect the detail to your answer.
She gives up her own activity to help someone.
ANSWER → EVIDENCE → EXPLAIN
Quote exactly or paraphrase accurately.
Use the strongest detail, not the longest paragraph.
Illustration and layout: Young reading detective magnifying glass over book and small scene child helping neighbor carry groceries. Three steps spacious readable.

Title (verbatim): VOCABULARY IN CONTEXT
Copy (verbatim):
Use nearby clues to unlock a word
DEFINITION — The text explains it.
Portable means easy to carry.
EXAMPLE — Examples reveal meaning.
Provisions: bread, fruit, and water.
CONTRAST — Opposites give clues.
Unlike the noisy hall, the room was tranquil.
SITUATION — Actions and events help.
She shivered and reached for a blanket.
READ AROUND IT → GUESS → SUBSTITUTE → CHECK
Choose the meaning that fits this passage.
Illustration and layout: Friendly word detective finding puzzle pieces; four panels with bag carried, hiking supplies, noisy hall vs peaceful room, chilly child blanket.
